newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Port Arthur killer jailed for term of natural life.
newsitem.headline: Port Arthur killer jailed for term of natural life.

text.p: An Australian court on Friday sentenced Port Arthur killer Martin Bryant to life in jail for the shooting massacre of 35 people last April, deeming him a pathetic misfit who nursed a grudge against the world.

Judge William Cox in the Tasmanian Supreme Court ordered that Bryant, 29, should be held in jail "for the term of his natural life", saying he feared the abnormal youth would forever remain a threat to society.

Bryant, who had confessed to unleashing modern Australia's worst mass murder among the ruins of an old penal colony in the state of Tasmania, told his lawyer later he was "happy" with the sentence, the lawyer, John Avery, told reporters.

But for Carolyn Loughton, who saw her 15-year-old daughter Sarah gunned down at the horrifying peak of the massacre at the Port Arthur historic site, the crimes called for the return of the death penalty in Australia.
"I think that all Australians should now look at the debate on the reintroduction of capital punishment for mass murder," she told reporters in a voice choked with emotion.

"They can look at making it retrospective to the 28th of April 1996 because our lives have been destroyed and that man has had seven months more life than my daughter .... He can rot in hell," she said.
In hearings this week, the court was told how Bryant killed 12 people in 15 seconds, shooting them as they sat having lunch in the site's crowded tourist cafe, ignoring pleas for mercy.

A total of 20 people died in the cafe, including Sarah Loughton, in what prosecutors called a horrifying slaughter during which Bryant laughed as he calmy walked around the tables shooting people in the head.

When Bryant was arrested the next morning after an all-night siege at a guesthouse near the Port Arthur ruins, another 15 people were dead, including a six-year-old girl executed as she hid behind a tree, her three-year-old sister and mother.
"Objectively, it is difficult to imagine a more chilling catalogue of crime," said Cox as he passed sentence.

Cox outlined how the massacre shocked the nation and its impact rippled out across the world. Four of the victims were Malaysian and Swiss tourists, and visitors from South Africa were among those who narrowly survived the rampage.

"The repercussion of this crime has been worldwide," Cox told the court. But he said Bryant was incapable of understanding the feelings of other people, was close to being mentally disabled and should be pitied.
"That the prisoner, through these handicaps ... has developed into a pathetic social misfit calls for understanding and pity, even though his actions demand condemnation," he said.
Grieving family of the dead wiped away tears as Bryant, who as usual seemed relaxed and willing to meet their stares from the public gallery, was taken from court for the last time.
Bryant is of severely limited intelligence and appears to suffer a rare and untreatable personality disorder called Asperger's Syndrome, the court heard this week.
But psychiatric reports quoted in court said Bryant was not criminally insane and knew right from wrong.

A desperate loner who inherited a fortune, Bryant nursed a deep grudge against society and vented it at Port Arthur in a rugged and picturesque part of the island where he and his family spent their weekends in his childhood.

He planned the massacre well in advance, cramming his yellow Volvo with three military-style rifles, rope, a hunting knife, handcuffs and cans of petrol for the hour-long drive to Port Arthur from his home of the state capital, Hobart, on April 28.

Bryant has disclosed his motive to Avery, but has sworn his lawyer to secrecy. Bryant is likely to one day divulge the trigger for his murderous rampage, Avery said, adding: "I don't think it's going to be any great surprise."
